title: An implemented Core member documents itself in the registry
scope:
where an *implemented* `Core` member's reference documentation lives, what `nvs meta --json`
emits, and how a consumer resolves a field both sources speak about. It does not decide named-argument
call syntax at a `Core` member — [0063](0063.md) R2 does, and the registry's
parameter names are that rule's home as much as this one's — nor the website's rendering, which
[website/README.md](../../website/README.md) owns, nor the spec's role as the member list, which
[0011](0011.md) § 2 deferred and
[0051](0051.md) § 3 placed, nor the API shape rules, which are
[0063](0063.md), nor where a *Novis* declaration's own documentation lives, which
is its `///` doc comment and is
[0137](0137.md) — a `Core` member is Rust and therefore
never carries one, which is why the two decisions do not overlap.

summary.headline: Every built-in carries its own reference card, next to its code
summary.body:
Each implemented member of the standard library declares its short description, its parameters,
its return value and the errors it throws in the same registry the runtime dispatches from, so
the documentation provably matches what ships. An enum carries one line per case, a constant one
sentence, and a member without a card fails the tests. `nvs meta --json` prints the whole
registry, and the reference pages are built from that alone. For a member not yet implemented
the design document is all there is; where both speak, the registry wins field by field.
